item.text: {"decisions":[{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:cursor:301c1497d14b1ed17100","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"The announcement credibly establishes present availability and workflow scope: Rollouts creates editable monitoring plans, compares post-deploy signals with a baseline, and can notify, pause, or propose a revert; Security Reviewer analyzes PRs and proposes fixes. Those post-PR agent roles are novel and directly relevant to small teams. Cursor sells the products, however, and supplies no sample, false-positive rate, regression rate, or independent outcome measure. Claims about catching regional regressions, distinguishing intended effects, and outperforming static analysis remain vendor claims. It overlaps GitHub’s separate security-autofix announcement but is not corroboration of it. Piece 01 can report availability, Piece 02 can test the claims against verification research, and Piece 03 can define a bounded pilot with approval gates." ,"version_id":"v-9e5e5fac9d48014feb9c5bfc"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:cursor:84d2e8f0655374a11ab2","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"This provides unusually concrete harness-engineering observations: Cursor reports a 66% system-prompt reduction, 46.9% fewer tokens in sessions that called an MCP tool after dynamic loading, and an overall 7% user-cost reduction without lower quality. Dynamic tool loading and context trimming are consequential for long-running agents and small-team budgets. Cursor has a commercial incentive to portray its harness as efficient, and the excerpt omits experiment size, duration, quality metric, confidence intervals, and the remainder of the tool-loading A/B results. These are cost/activity measures, not accepted software outcomes. The item is distinct from product-feature announcements. Piece 01 can describe the harness change, Piece 02 can scrutinize the internal measurements, and Piece 03 can motivate local cost-and-quality instrumentation." ,"version_id":"v-5fed8f79222f91b61985792d"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"feed:github:7a6dc2d18f9ec533b042","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The usable fact is limited to Gemini 4 Argon’s rollout, plan eligibility, usage-based billing, and administrator controls in Copilot. The performance language—more tasks solved on every benchmark and thorough checking of edge cases—has no named benchmark, task count, baseline, score, or inspection method. GitHub and Google benefit commercially from model adoption, and the item depends on the underlying Google model release rather than independent testing. It is routine model-picker coverage and duplicates the broader availability story without a demonstrated workflow consequence, so it falls under the policy’s exclusion of model-release scorekeeping without usable evidence." ,"version_id":"v-9e3b7675dd5b66ce334d1e75"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:independent-research-authors:258392c93310baab1471","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"AgentSWE offers a novel, inspectable evaluation design for a production-relevant delegation problem: 25 creation, editing, and optimization commissions are developed against visible examples but accepted on frozen submissions and held-out, requirement-derived tests. The reported failure modes—visible-case overfitting, hollow runtimes, and unsupported completion claims—directly inform verification practices. The benchmark authors have an incentive to establish the importance of their benchmark, and 25 agent-building tasks are too narrow to generalize to ordinary application work; the excerpt also gives no per-agent outcome table. It is distinct from harness-construction benchmarks. Piece 02 can examine the demonstration-versus-delivery gap, and Piece 03 can recommend held-out acceptance checks and explicit completion gates." ,"version_id":"v-b8c088105e97e9e6f3ce9ed9"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:independent-research-authors:337cbc4cedf5cfb1d758","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"The useful contribution is its explicit synthesis of conflicting evidence: field experiments, a small randomized trial, repository studies, and practitioner judgment measure different populations and outcomes, so throughput claims need not imply lower review or rework costs. The cited older results must be labeled as background rather than new October findings, and their numerical claims should be checked in the primary studies before publication. The paper is argumentative, and its assertion that model limitations cannot be eliminated by training is not established by the supplied passage; its authors benefit academically from a strong thesis. It overlaps verification research but broadens the comparison to organizational outcomes. Piece 02 can map the disagreement and measurement differences; Piece 03 can present persistent specifications and process artifacts as a bounded hypothesis, not a proven cure." ,"version_id":"v-2c06c266b5857581b3f3c253"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:independent-research-authors:89ac63769de00fed6835","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"This supplies original qualitative evidence about supervision as a connected workflow rather than a final review step. Observations and workflow diagrams from 19 experienced developers support a seven-stage framework and identify concrete practices: concentrating effort in planning, delegating some checking to other agents, and converting recurring guidance into reusable assets. The sample is small and self-selected, Reddit discussions are not outcome validation, and the study does not show that any practice reduces defects or time. The authors have an academic incentive to validate their framework, but no stated tool-selling interest. It complements rather than independently corroborates AgentSWE. Piece 02 can locate where verification work moves, and Piece 03 can turn the stages into a small-team pilot checklist while acknowledging the qualitative boundary." ,"version_id":"v-9bde3907428df8ef68a78026"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"feed:sourcegraph:ea3179ffe2d4c95b4f7b","piece_ids":[],"reason":"Scheduled triggers, telemetry-driven tasks, and callable agent functions are relevant watch-list concepts, but the article is chiefly a product vision. Claims that prompt-to-PR is essentially solved, model quality has plateaued, and brownfield maintenance remains completely unsolved rest on personal impressions and unnamed conversations, with no cases, measurements, or reproducible artifact. Sourcegraph sells tools in this market and benefits from framing the next battleground around autonomous codebases. The vision overlaps Cursor’s concrete rollout-monitoring announcement but does not independently support it. Because its novel elements are speculative rather than observed capabilities or bounded practitioner results, it is not strong enough for any piece." ,"version_id":"v-1c7d0d28b27050f0e12c26c2"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"podcast:infoq:5925e1fbf36f4960a85e","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The discussion raises relevant issues—ambiguous requirements, comprehensive tests, review burden, legacy-system uncertainty, and possible skill atrophy—but presents them as expert judgment without a named production case, sample, comparison, or measured outcome. The speaker and publisher benefit from attention, even though no direct tool sale is apparent. Its main observations substantially duplicate the stronger AgentSWE and supervision studies, while the claim that code review is ineffective is too broad for the support shown. The transcript makes the opinion inspectable, but it adds too little novel evidence to the selected portfolio; rejection is an editorial choice, not a judgment that the interview is generally unreliable." ,"version_id":"v-36b84d40a169e2446f129e9d"},{"decision":"defer","item_id":"podcast:infoq:5950b2ca18b6b0b75291","piece_ids":[],"reason":"Psychological safety and team alignment could materially affect small-team adoption, and this is a useful perspective not captured by tool benchmarks. However, the excerpt provides no survey, adoption comparison, named team episode, or other observation linking psychological safety to successful agent use. Its technical claims about overwhelming review volume, junior training, and verification tooling also overlap the other InfoQ interview and accepted workflow evidence. The guest and publisher have attention incentives, though no explicit product result is being sold. Defer until a documented team case, study, or clearly bounded firsthand incident shows how the proposed practices changed reporting, review, defects, or adoption behavior." ,"version_id":"v-dfc85ba89acbfb7e4e48eb77"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"youtube:9yPyoxlyc5Q","piece_ids":["03"],"reason":"The transcript contains a concrete practitioner demonstration on a named real repository issue: a reusable skill explores the task with a subagent, asks structured questions about selectors and edge cases, and uses issues and worktrees to coordinate execution. That makes the observation useful as a low-cost requirements-clarification tactic. It is still a single creator-reported example with no before/after outcome, defect rate, or evidence that the resulting change was accepted. The creator benefits from attention to a popular skills repository, and the GitHub-hosted event is not independent evidence of Copilot effectiveness. It overlaps the supervision research but supplies an operational example. Use only in Piece 03 as a pilot technique, not a production-readiness result." ,"version_id":"v-ab01f07d4890bf0557ad681d"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"youtube:hTAWHgQI4xg","piece_ids":[],"reason":"Spec-driven work and the shift from implementation toward orchestration are audience-relevant themes, but the supporting claims are not inspectable: weeks or months of work allegedly becoming minutes, whole features being delegated, and a pilot running agents for multiple roles lack named tasks, baselines, acceptance criteria, and outcomes. IBM has commercial interests in AI adoption, while the video format also rewards confident, attention-getting generalization. The advice duplicates stronger evidence on requirements, supervision, and held-out verification without adding a reproducible case or novel limitation. It therefore cannot support a production-readiness conclusion or an actionable recommendation." ,"version_id":"v-470d183469c7db5d35e05d67"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"youtube:7XzjQa8z0uc","piece_ids":[],"reason":"This is a beginner-oriented walkthrough using a toy cookie-shop game. It can demonstrate interface mechanics such as projects, Git, multiple agents, skills, and cloud handoff, but it provides no production task, team workflow, review outcome, security boundary, or reliability measurement. The creator benefits from tutorial attention, and the demonstration depends on OpenAI’s product claims rather than independently testing them. It is also directly within the policy’s exclusion of beginner prompting and setup tutorials, and it duplicates official Codex capability announcements without adding production evidence." ,"version_id":"v-fe38088af4757b05a5b066aa"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"youtube:IZXv6a78NDw","piece_ids":["01","03"],"reason":"The official demonstration credibly establishes workflow scope and release status: GitHub code review is generally available, GitLab support is preview, initial cloud reviews can run automatically, and reviewers can combine PR context with private chat, skills, connectors, custom instructions, and a separate local pass. These are relevant workflow changes for small teams. OpenAI sells Codex, and the video provides no review-accuracy, defect-catch, latency, or human-time comparison; the title’s assertion that review is no longer the bottleneck is therefore unusable. It is distinct from GitHub’s alert-remediation agent, which fixes CodeQL alerts rather than reviewing arbitrary PRs. Piece 01 can report the capability and Piece 03 can propose a measured, human-approved trial." ,"version_id":"v-aa6fb499336c3701ec05174c"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"youtube:PUBc2G0Tj5E","piece_ids":["01","03"],"reason":"The video directly demonstrates a newly integrated multi-agent CLI workflow: parallel tasks across projects, status navigation, follow-up messages, conversation forks into worktrees, remote control, activity analytics, and terminal rendering. Worktree isolation and task visibility are relevant to small-team delegation. The evidence is an official vendor demo on toy burrito projects; it does not state rollout scope, quantify reliability, or show merge-quality and conflict outcomes. OpenAI benefits commercially, and this should not be treated as independent production validation. It overlaps general multi-agent tutorials but is the primary capability demonstration. Piece 01 can describe the workflow change; Piece 03 can identify worktree isolation, permission boundaries, and completion quality as local pilot checks." ,"version_id":"v-f95ed73f67d6b610264834f4"},{"decision":"defer","item_id":"youtube:J9NQTYUP6k0","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The suggested brief—task, guardrails, and definition of done—is relevant, but the headline claim about how the top 1% work and the assertion that plan mode is no longer useful are based on secondhand references to Hacker News and a conference talk. The primary passages, dates, model versions, sample definition, and outcomes are not supplied, and behavior may change across model releases. The creator benefits from attention and packages scattered advice as a trend; it also conflicts with accepted evidence favoring up-front clarification without providing a comparable test. Defer until the primary statements and applicable versions are inspectable or a controlled comparison measures planning versus outcome-based briefing." ,"version_id":"v-8bb3472c3858254a3ab9d00e"},{"decision":"defer","item_id":"feed:arxiv-research-authors:1abee7324728c1791690","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The trajectory audit and intervention are potentially important: reported shortcut attempts are frequent, network isolation is insufficient, and an independence instruction sharply reduces attempts while reportedly preserving task performance. However, the arXiv identifier indicates a September submission while the supplied publication field is October 15, suggesting a revision or feed date. No version history identifies whether the audit results or intervention are new within the mechanical 30-date window. The authors also benefit academically from motivating exploit-aware evaluation, and LLM-judge validity and exact trajectory counts need inspection. Defer until the original date and revision diff are available; accept only if these findings first appeared inside the window." ,"version_id":"v-45f4534cc92ac359acad76b3"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:arxiv-research-authors:7e1b631b4402773a85d0","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"SWE-Nexus presents a novel, inspectable way to construct repository tasks from observed test execution, including counterfactual masking, revalidation of composed scopes, 600 tasks from 105 repositories in six languages, and evaluation of 12 models under three scaffolds. The best one-attempt resolution rate of 37.8% usefully bounds current capability on these generated tasks. The benchmark authors have an incentive to emphasize their method, and traced test coverage is not equivalent to full production intent; repository selection, task difficulty, and per-language results are absent from the excerpt. It complements rather than corroborates requirement-derived AgentSWE. Piece 02 can compare evaluation designs, while Piece 03 can make execution-grounded acceptance and partial scoring watch signals." ,"version_id":"v-d626cb5ce8d4fa2b3e4b2074"},{"decision":"reject","item_id":"feed:arxiv-research-authors:a3006b90b025ce476489","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The study has substantial empirical detail—130,000 comments, 72 classifiers, reported F1 scores, and a 30-person user study—but it concerns offensive-language moderation in software communities, not the adoption, verification, cost, security, or maintenance of coding agents. Large language models appear only as a future research direction. The authors have the usual incentive to demonstrate their proposed moderation system, and neither its novel results nor its limitations resolve the publication’s central question. It does not duplicate an included coding-agent announcement; it is simply out of scope." ,"version_id":"v-4172c5815087cb6aba260466"},{"decision":"defer","item_id":"feed:arxiv-research-authors:b0eb86463b6611a88d0b","piece_ids":[],"reason":"The execution-grounded, torch-free verifier and whole-repository migration results would be highly relevant, particularly the gap between high specification pass rates and behavioral equivalence and the reported TWINHARNESS improvement. Yet arXiv identifier 2605 shows that the work originated in May, while the supplied October 15 date appears to be a later revision or feed event. The excerpt does not say which claims, tasks, or results were added during the 30-date window. The benchmark authors also benefit from showing their harness improves performance. Defer pending version history and a revision diff; reconsider if the execution results or harness experiment are demonstrably new, otherwise the item fails freshness despite its quality." ,"version_id":"v-cbadc131b54f9c609fb1f48b"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:arxiv-research-authors:e81252ca071140d1abb1","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"Doc2Harness directly tests a neglected production variable: whether models can build the harness around an agent. Its two-stage isolation, frozen candidates, scripted mock model, four observable scoring channels, positive controls, 328 tests, 19 models, and three builds per model provide a comparatively inspectable method. The reported 53.05% best pass rate supports only the bounded conclusion that cross-cutting harness implementation remains difficult. Benchmark authors have an academic incentive to establish novelty, and scripted models plus contract reconstruction do not measure ordinary application development or live-model behavior. It is distinct from AgentSWE’s agent-building commissions and SWE-Nexus task construction. Piece 02 can scrutinize harness claims; Piece 03 can recommend deterministic harness tests and watch failure clusters." ,"version_id":"v-04e52f11243b49bafc9d3927"},{"decision":"defer","item_id":"feed:github:d90685b190262b176e08","piece_ids":[],"reason":"A dated model deprecation is operationally relevant to teams with pinned workflows, and GitHub is the authoritative source for its own schedule. However, the supplied passage omits the actual list of models after saying the following models will be deprecated; only an exception for Claude Opus 4.8 remains visible. Without the affected names, teams cannot assess exposure or alternatives. GitHub has a commercial interest in moving users to supported models, and this is a maintenance notice rather than evidence of capability. Defer until the complete model list and suggested replacements are captured; then it may warrant a concise Piece 03 migration note." ,"version_id":"v-48c771d9cad659bfe55774d1"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:github:f6a9ed9af548e96e0a77","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"This is a consequential, well-bounded availability claim: GitHub’s agent can explore a repository, propose a fix for a default-branch code-scanning alert, rerun CodeQL, iterate, and open a draft PR; the notice also specifies batch limits, policy controls, plan requirements, AI-credit consumption, and Actions cost. GitHub sells the required security and Copilot services. A clean CodeQL rerun shows that the targeted alert closed, not that the patch is exploit-resistant, regression-free, or maintainable; no false-fix or acceptance outcomes are reported. It overlaps Cursor Security Reviewer but represents a separate product and is not corroboration. Piece 01 reports GA, Piece 02 separates validation from correctness, and Piece 03 defines review, regression, budget, and rollback gates." ,"version_id":"v-c7fa3f0d4656b8a511da76d6"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:infoq:11afb59991f162853855","piece_ids":["02","03"],"reason":"The item identifies meaningful benchmark changes—long-horizon tasks, agent-based evaluation, continuous scoring across functionality, visual fidelity, regressions, and structural constraints—and reports a useful task boundary: new deterministic transformations appear easier than refactoring, runtime validation, and framework changes. However, InfoQ is summarizing Google’s benchmark, so this is not independent corroboration; Google and participating model providers have incentives around their tools. The excerpt omits the number and distribution of long-horizon tasks, making the 32% pass rate and 80% completion example unsafe to generalize. It complements the research benchmarks with mobile-development tasks. Piece 02 can compare what the scoring captures and misses, while Piece 03 can suggest task-class-specific pilots and runtime checks." ,"version_id":"v-0ba58a184ce4146081b2020d"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:infoq:37901f78ed2a5174f519","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"This is a valuable production case because it pairs scale claims with a concrete failure and response. Spotify reportedly grew monthly merged changes from about 8,100 to 17,000, uses agents for fleet maintenance and migrations, and experienced an automated dependency upgrade that passed checks but failed in production, prompting stronger safeguards, rollback capacity, and working-hours scheduling. Merged changes are activity, not accepted quality, and the excerpt does not isolate AI’s causal contribution. InfoQ depends primarily on Spotify’s self-report, while Spotify benefits reputationally; social-media reactions are commentary, not corroboration. Piece 01 shows scaled maintenance automation, Piece 02 exposes the throughput-versus-stability distinction, and Piece 03 supports monitoring, staged rollout, ownership, and rollback practices." ,"version_id":"v-0adab8a5a121a93d9b20d967"},{"decision":"accept","item_id":"feed:infoq:53beeea632eecd42bb0a","piece_ids":["01","02","03"],"reason":"The migration is a concrete production example with defined scope and process: more than 800,000 lines were replaced over roughly 14.5 weeks through 128 incremental PRs while releases continued, using compatibility layers, end-to-end tests, compilation, and human review. The reported 5.25-second-to-292-millisecond scenario is specific enough to retain as a vendor-reported measurement, although hardware and run distribution are missing; 87.1% clean cargo checks measure compilation activity, not behavioral correctness. InfoQ’s account depends on GitHub’s self-report, and GitHub benefits from showcasing Copilot; community reactions add concerns, not independent outcomes. Piece 01 covers the capability, Piece 02 examines verification limits, and Piece 03 derives incremental cutover and boundary-testing practices." ,"version_id":"v-1d0c46de7ab29e24cb9194da"}]}
